newsitem.title: USA: Experts differ on import of Clinton's agenda.
newsitem.headline: Experts differ on import of Clinton's agenda.

text.p: With a political deftness often obscured by the constant controversy swirling around him, President Bill Clinton is spinning a web of arrangements for the 21st Century that boosters say will long endure.

The Democrat's critics say these arrangements, which so far include a deal with Republicans to balance the budget by 2002 and an accomodation with Russia on NATO expansion, merely ratify the status quo and leave big issues unresolved.

These include how to pay for retirement and health care benefits when the U.S. baby boom generation begins leaving the workforce early in the next century, and how to preserve Russia's fragile experiment in democracy.

Conversations with Clinton aides suggest that there is no appetite for tackling these issues any time soon. So what else is involved in Clinton's second-term agenda, how does he hope to make his mark on history?

"His agenda is the agenda of any president who does not control Congress -- try to find some common ground and get what he can. I think it's the only strategy he has unless he wants four years of bitter partisan warfare," said historian Michael Riccards, the president of Fitchburg State College in Massachusetts.

Over the next week, Clinton will unveil a set of proposals consistent with the budget agreement, starting with a science and technology initiative that he will offer in a commencement speech at Maryland's Morgan State University on Sunday.

He will meet U.S. business executives a few days later to talk about how to move poor people from welfare to work as a strict new welfare law requires, and host a town hall meeting in West Virginia as part of his crusade to improve education.

Clinton then goes to Europe to sign the concordat between NATO and Russia and celebrate the 50th anniversary of the U.S. Marshal Plan, which helped underwrite European reconstruction after the Second World War.

"Clinton's second term quite literally is about getting set for the 21st Century," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said. "Just as (former President Ronald) Reagan dismantled the structures of the Cold War, Clinton wants to be remembered as the guy who was the architect for what came afterward."

"You know, it's a pretty impressive achievement to go through this dramatic a period of change and to do so with as much stability and security as the American people are currently enjoying. If we sustain that in the 21st century, it will be a remarkable achievement," he said.

McCurry, interviewed in his White House office at the end of the day the NATO-Russia agreement was announced, said the endless drumbeat of scandalous allegations about Clinton's campaign financing and Arkansas past was having little impact.

"It has failed to penetrate the consciousness of the country and it has failed to deter Clinton from pursuing the agenda he thinks he was elected to pursue," he said, pointing to Clinton's continued strong approval rating in the polls.
But Bruce Buchanan, a political science professor at the University of Texas, called the allegations "latent landmines that at a minimum are likely to provide future occasions for embarrassment."

White House sources said Clinton was close to moving unilaterally to dampen the campaign financing controversy. If Congress fails to heed his call for reform legislation by the Fourth of July -- U.S. Independence Day -- he will petition the Federal Election Commission to ban so-called "soft money," the sources said.
Under current law, political parties can accept unlimited contributions -- "soft money" -- and use the funds as they see fit with little outside regulation.
